items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a model (1909) proposing that industry locates where total transport costs of raw materials and finished products are lowest”.
items.answer: Weber’s least-cost theory
items.markingKey: Weber’s least-cost theory: a model (1909) proposing that industry locates where total transport costs of raw materials and finished products are lowest. [1]

items.stem: Explain Weber’s least-cost theory of industrial location.
items.answer: Firms seek the location with lowest total transport costs of materials and products; weight-losing industries locate near materials, weight-gaining near markets; labour cost savings or agglomeration may justify moving away from the least-transport-cost point.

items.stem: Explain why transport costs are less important for manufacturing location today.
items.answer: Containerisation, bulk carriers and better roads have cut costs; products are lighter and higher value; labour costs, skills, government incentives and markets now dominate.

items.stem: Making 1 tonne of steel uses 1.3 t of iron ore and 1 t of coking coal. Transport costs $1 per tonne-km for all goods. Distances (km) from each possible site to the iron ore source, the coking coal source and the market: site X (at the iron ore mine): 0, 172, 293; site Y (at the coking coal source): 115, 0, 240; site Z (at the market): 264, 187, 0. Suggest why the firm might not choose the least-cost site.
items.answer: Cheaper or more skilled labour elsewhere; government grants or tax breaks; agglomeration economies; land availability; energy prices; political stability.

(a) Calculate the material index and state what it suggests about location. (b) Suggest why the firm might not choose the least-cost site.
items.answer: (a) 1.6: weight-losing, so a location near raw materials is favoured. (b) Cheaper or more skilled labour elsewhere; government grants or tax breaks; agglomeration economies; land availability; energy prices; political stability.

items.stem: “Weber’s least-cost theory is no longer useful in explaining the location of manufacturing industry.” How far do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: Transport costs are now small; labour, skills, markets, government policy, globalisation and behavioural factors dominate; most modern industry is footloose. Against: Heavy, weight-losing industries (steel, cement, aluminium smelting near cheap power) still follow least-cost principles; the idea of cost minimisation remains central to TNC decisions. Conclusion: The theory’s assumptions are outdated, but its central idea of minimising costs still helps explain some industries.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “Weber’s least-cost theory”?
options: A model (1909) proposing that industry locates where total transport costs of raw materials and finished products are lowest.
An industry in which the product weighs less than the raw materials, such as steel or sugar refining.
The weight of localised raw materials divided by the weight of the finished product; above 1 suggests a location near raw materials.
An industry that is not tied to raw materials or markets and can locate in many places.

items.stem: Explain the importance of agglomeration economies.
items.answer: Firms share suppliers, skilled labour pools, infrastructure and knowledge; clusters such as Silicon Valley or the Pearl River Delta attract further investment.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the long-term decline of manufacturing employment and output in an area or country”.
items.answer: Deindustrialisation
items.markingKey: Deindustrialisation: the long-term decline of manufacturing employment and output in an area or country. [1]

items.stem: Explain the causes of deindustrialisation in HICs.
items.answer: Competition from lower-wage countries; automation; exhaustion of resources (coal); old plant and infrastructure; high labour and land costs; strong currencies; shift of investment to services; TNC relocation.

items.stem: Explain the impacts of deindustrialisation on a region.
items.answer: Unemployment and loss of skilled jobs; out-migration and population decline; derelict land; multiplier effect reduces services; social problems; but cleaner environment and regeneration opportunities.

items.stem: Table 19.2 shows employment (millions) in a country. National total 25, of which manufacturing 2.6. Regions (total, manufacturing): Region A: 1.66, 0.19; Region B: 2.4, 0.35; Region C: 1.68, 0.34; Region D: 3.2, 0.57. LQ = (regional manufacturing ÷ regional total) ÷ (national manufacturing ÷ national total). Suggest why regions with high LQs for manufacturing may be badly affected by deindustrialisation.
items.answer: They depend heavily on one sector, so closures cause high unemployment, multiplier effects and out-migration; skills may not suit new jobs.

items.stem: Assess the view that the global shift of manufacturing has had more advantages than disadvantages for LICs and NICs.
items.answer: For: Jobs, export earnings, FDI, skills and infrastructure; rapid growth in China, South Korea, Vietnam and Bangladesh; poverty reduction. Against: Low wages and poor conditions (Rana Plaza 2013), pollution, dependence on TNCs, profits leaving the country, footloose plants relocating, inequality between regions. Conclusion: For many countries the advantages have been large, but they depend on upgrading skills and protecting workers and the environment.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “an area with tax breaks, relaxed regulations and good infrastructure to attract foreign investment, such as Shenzhen (1980)”.
items.answer: Special economic zone (SEZ)
items.markingKey: Special economic zone (SEZ): an area with tax breaks, relaxed regulations and good infrastructure to attract foreign investment, such as Shenzhen (1980). [1]

items.stem: Explain how governments attract manufacturing investment.
items.answer: Tax holidays and grants; SEZs and EPZs with infrastructure; low tariffs on imported components; relaxed regulations; trained labour; political stability; trade agreements.

items.stem: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of special economic zones.
items.answer: Advantages: FDI, jobs, exports, technology transfer, infrastructure (Shenzhen grew from a fishing town to over 17 million people). Disadvantages: loss of tax revenue, exploitation of workers, pollution, regional inequality, enclaves with few local links.

items.stem: A government gave a foreign car-parts company US$40 million in grants and tax relief to open a factory in an EPZ in Kenya. The factory employs 3 000 people at an average wage of US$2 500 a year. The regional employment multiplier is estimated at 2.2. The company agreed to stay for at least 10 years. Calculate the total wages paid to direct employees over 10 years.

A government gave a foreign car-parts company US$90 million in grants and tax relief to open a factory in an SEZ in India. The factory employs 3 000 people at an average wage of US$3 000 a year. The regional employment multiplier is estimated at 2.1. The company agreed to stay for at least 10 years. (a) Calculate the incentive cost per direct job. (b) Calculate the total wages paid to direct employees over 10 years.
To what extent do you agree that government policy is the most important factor in the growth of manufacturing in NICs?
items.answer: For: Planning, SEZs, export promotion, education and infrastructure investment drove growth in South Korea, Taiwan and China. Against: Low labour costs, TNC investment, global markets, location on trade routes, culture and timing were also important; some policies failed (ISI in Latin America). Conclusion: Policy was crucial in creating the conditions for growth, but it worked because it exploited global market opportunities and low-cost labour.

items.stem: Explain why governments may try to manage industrial decline.
items.answer: To reduce unemployment and social problems, retrain workers, attract new industries, regenerate derelict areas and reduce regional inequality.

items.stem: A government gave a foreign car-parts company US$60 million in grants and tax relief to open a factory in an SEZ in India. The factory employs 800 people at an average wage of US$3 000 a year. The regional employment multiplier is estimated at 2.1. The company agreed to stay for at least 5 years. Explain why the multiplier effect creates additional jobs.
items.answer: The factory buys components and services from local suppliers, and employees spend wages in local shops, creating indirect and induced jobs; tax revenue funds services.

items.stem: A government gave a foreign car-parts company US$20 million in grants and tax relief to open a factory in an EPZ in Kenya. (a) Calculate the total wages paid to direct employees over 10 years. (b) Evaluate the use of such incentives to attract manufacturing.
items.answer: (a) US$20 000 000 (b) They bring jobs, skills and investment, but are costly per job, may attract footloose firms that leave when incentives end, and may simply move jobs from other regions.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “special economic zone (SEZ)”?
options: An industrial estate where imported components are assembled for export with tax and tariff exemptions.
An area with tax breaks, relaxed regulations and good infrastructure to attract foreign investment, such as Shenzhen (1980).
Protecting domestic industries with tariffs so they can replace imports.
Government strategies to promote particular industries or regions.
items.answer: An area with tax breaks, relaxed regulations and good infrastructure to attract foreign investment, such as Shenzhen (1980).

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Tax incentives always create long-term jobs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Footloose firms may leave when incentives end.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “Government policy has played a major role in the growth of NICs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the advantages and disadvantages of special economic zones.
items.answer: (a) Correct. South Korea and China used planning, SEZs, credit and protection. Disadvantages: loss of tax revenue, exploitation of workers, pollution, regional inequality, enclaves with few local links.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “an industry in which the product weighs less than the raw materials, such as steel or sugar refining”.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain Weber’s least-cost theory of industrial location. (b) Explain the importance of agglomeration economies.
items.answer: (a) Firms seek the location with lowest total transport costs of materials and products; weight-losing industries locate near materials, weight-gaining near markets; labour cost savings or agglomeration may justify moving away from the least-transport-cost point. (b) Firms share suppliers, skilled labour pools, infrastructure and knowledge; clusters such as Silicon Valley or the Pearl River Delta attract further investment.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the importance of agglomeration economies. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Footloose industries must locate near raw materials.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Firms share suppliers, skilled labour pools, infrastructure and knowledge; clusters such as Silicon Valley or the Pearl River Delta attract further investment. (b) Not correct. They have freedom of location.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Making 1 tonne of aluminium uses 1.7 t of alumina and 0.2 t of carbon anodes. Transport costs $1 per tonne-km for all goods. items.answer: 1.9: weight-losing, so a location near raw materials is favoured.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that Weber’s least-cost theory is no longer useful in explaining the location of manufacturing industry?
items.answer: For: Transport costs are now small; labour, skills, markets, government policy, globalisation and behavioural factors dominate; most modern industry is footloose. Against: Heavy, weight-losing industries (steel, cement, aluminium smelting near cheap power) still follow least-cost principles; the idea of cost minimisation remains central to TNC decisions. Conclusion: The theory’s assumptions are outdated, but its central idea of minimising costs still helps explain some industries.

items.answer: (a) Correct. In much of sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia most workers are informal. (b) Not correct. Output may stay high with fewer workers through automation.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A revision website states: “Manufacturing employment in the UK peaked in the 1960s.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why the informal sector is large in many LIC cities.
items.answer: (a) Correct. It has fallen since, from about 9 million to under 3 million. (b) Rapid urban growth exceeds formal job creation; low skills; easy entry with little capital; regulations and taxes avoided; provides flexible income for migrants.

items.stem: Table 19.2 shows employment (millions) in a country. National total 32, of which manufacturing 4.8. Regions (total, manufacturing): Region A: 1.82, 0.09; Region B: 3.77, 0.86; Region C: 3.19, 0.16; Region D: 1.09, 0.16. LQ = (regional manufacturing ÷ regional total) ÷ (national manufacturing ÷ national total). Identify the region most specialised in manufacturing and state what its LQ shows.
items.answer: Region B: LQ 1.52, so its share of manufacturing employment is 1.52 times the national share.
